KEY MESSAGE 1...

After some isolated diurnally driven showers and thunderstorms
this afternoon, ridging becomes established over the western
Atlantic downstream of a split flow pattern. While a broad 
northern branch trough tracks through southern Canada, a cut-
off low in the southern branch slowly tracks through the
Midwest. As was discussed in the previous discussion, there
remains discrepancies on whether these two features phase or
not tomorrow into tomorrow night which will determine where the
heavy rainfall axis sets-up. Latest trends still indicate the
northern branch will help focus and direct the initial moisture
axis and forcing for ascent around the Saint Lawrence River 
Valley tomorrow, supporting periods of rain and thunderstorms.
While the most widespread rain/storms looks to occur mainly 
west of eastern NY, a few weak embedded shortwaves tracking 
within the strengthening south to southwesterly flow over the 
Northeast will likely support scattered showers and 
thunderstorms. As the northern and southern branch features 
interact, a nearly full latitude trough develops upstream, 
allowing the wind regime to tap into the Gulf and advect a very
moisture rich air mass into the Northeast. In fact, PWATs 
increase towards 2" or within the 99th percentile of the NAEFS 
model climatology for this time of year. Thus, any isolated to
scattered thunderstorms that develop will be capable of
producing heavy downpours. With 20-30kts of deep layer shear, cannot
completely rule out brief damaging winds from any storm that can
grow upscale; however, ample cloud coverage in a highly moist
environment should keep lapse rates weak and thus limit instability,
keeping any severe storms isolated. We are not currently outlook
in SPC's Day 2 Convective Outlook but remain in general thunder.

Heading into Sunday night, the northern branch in southern
Canada looks to slow down and strengthen, even taking on a 
negative tilt while the once cut-off low escapes into the TN 
Valley and weakens as it becomes sheared out. Latest guidance 
shows a jet streak over the Northeast developing Sunday night
with the continued unidirectional southerly winds over the 
Northeast maintaining a rich supply of warm air and moisture 
advection. Showers and embedded convection expand eastward 
Sunday night into eastern NY and western New England ahead of 
the approaching parent trough; however, there is increasing 
consensus in a secondary sfc low developing in the favorable 
equatorward entrance region of the jet streak. Where this 
feature develops will be key as it looks to focus the 
moisture/forcing leading to a heavy rain axis late Sunday night
into Monday morning. There remains discrepancies on where this 
axis develops with one cluster favoring the mid-Hudson Valley, 
NW CT into New England while a second cluster shows it further 
northwest into more of eastern NY. 

Given the recent heavy/locally extreme rainfall much of
eastern NY experienced this past week, most soils are saturated
and rivers/streams are elevated. 1hr and 3hr flash flood
guidance values remain low ranging from 1 to 2.5 inches so if
these values are exceeded, flash flooding concerns will 
increase. Given the anticipated highly moisture rich environment
with forecast soundings showing high freezing heights 12-13kft 
and tall/skinny CAPE, efficient warm rain processes will be at 
play likely supporting high rainfall rates, especially within 
the heavy rain axis. However, unlike the recent heavy rain 
event, this seems to be a more progressive pattern as the trough
continues to swing eastward into Monday. Thus, even if heavy 
rain can persist over a given area, it does not look to last 
multiple hours which lowers the potential for widespread 
flooding concerns. In addition, latest probabilistic guidance 
shows just a few isolated spots with very low values for 24hr 
rain amounts between 8PM Sunday and 8PM Monday exceeding 2 
inches with even the 90th percentile for most of eastern NY and 
western New England under 2 inches in 24hrs. Therefore, WPC maintained
its marginal to slight risk for excessive rainfall in the Day 3
Outlook (12 UTC Mon to 12 UTC Tues) messaging isolated to 
scattered flash flooding. The slight risk is focused in the eastern
Catskills, mid-Hudson Valley and NW CT where the heavy rain 
axis looks to set-up late Sunday night into Monday but given 
continued discrepancies on the exact placement, this could 
change in future updates. Regardless of the slight risk 
location, it is important to be prepared for the potential for 
isolated to scattered flash flooding Sunday night into Monday in
eastern NY and western New England. Areas that were hard hit 
with heavy rain this past week will be most vulnerable to 
renewed flooding concerns.
